title: Maternal and Child Health Nursing (Midwifery)
description: Antenatal care, normal labour and delivery, postnatal and newborn care, obstetric emergencies, and care of the sick child.

topics.title: Antenatal Care
topics.summary: Booking, schedule of contacts, investigations, supplements and danger signs in pregnancy.

notes.b: Antenatal care (ANC) aims to promote maternal and fetal health, detect and manage complications and prepare for birth. WHO (2016) recommends at least eight contacts, with the first before 12 weeks. At booking: history (obstetric, medical, social), estimation of gestational age from the last menstrual period (Naegele's rule: EDD = LMP + 9 months + 7 days) and early ultrasound, examination, and investigations — haemoglobin/PCV, blood group and Rhesus, haemoglobin genotype, HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis, urinalysis (protein, glucose), and where indicated blood glucose. Each visit: weight, blood pressure, urinalysis for protein, symphysis–fundal height (in cm ≈ gestational weeks from about 24 weeks), fetal heart and movements, presentation.
k: Booking tests: Hb, group, genotype, HIV, HBV, syphilis

notes.b: Routine interventions: iron (30–60 mg) and folic acid (400 µg) supplementation; tetanus–diphtheria (Td) vaccination; intermittent preventive treatment of malaria with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) from 13 weeks, given monthly (at least three doses), with long-lasting insecticidal nets; deworming after the first trimester; PMTCT (lifelong ART for HIV-positive women); nutritional and birth preparedness counselling, including a plan for skilled birth attendance. Danger signs requiring urgent care: vaginal bleeding, severe headache or blurred vision, convulsions, fever, severe abdominal pain, fast or difficult breathing, reduced fetal movements, leaking of fluid, and swelling of the face and hands.

topics.title: Normal Labour and Delivery
topics.summary: Stages of labour, the partograph, mechanism of labour, and active management of the third stage.

notes.b: Labour is regular painful uterine contractions leading to progressive cervical effacement and dilatation. First stage: latent phase (cervix up to about 5 cm, slower) and active phase (from about 5 cm to full dilatation at 10 cm — WHO now considers ≥ 5 cm as active phase); monitoring includes fetal heart rate (every 15–30 minutes in the first stage), contractions, maternal vital signs, cervical dilatation and descent (vaginal examinations about every 4 hours). The WHO partograph/Labour Care Guide records progress; crossing the alert line prompts closer review or referral. Second stage: from full dilatation to delivery of the baby. Third stage: from delivery of the baby to delivery of the placenta and membranes. Fourth stage: the first hour or two after delivery (observe for haemorrhage).

The mechanism of labour for a vertex (occipitoanterior) presentation: engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension (crowning and birth of the head), restitution, external rotation, and birth of the shoulders and body. Episiotomy is not routine. Active management of the third stage of labour (AMTSL) prevents postpartum haemorrhage: give a uterotonic within 1 minute of birth (oxytocin 10 IU IM is first-line; misoprostol orally where oxytocin is unavailable), controlled cord traction, and uterine massage/monitoring of tone; delayed cord clamping (1–3 minutes) benefits the baby. Examine the placenta for completeness. Immediate newborn care: dry and stimulate, skin-to-skin contact, early breastfeeding within one hour, clean cord care (chlorhexidine), vitamin K, eye prophylaxis and birth-dose vaccines.

topics.title: Obstetric Emergencies
topics.summary: Postpartum haemorrhage, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, obstructed labour, sepsis and neonatal resuscitation.

notes.b: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is blood loss ≥ 500 mL within 24 hours after birth (≥ 1,000 mL severe). Causes — the 4 Ts: Tone (uterine atony — commonest), Trauma (tears, rupture), Tissue (retained placenta) and Thrombin (coagulopathy). Management: call for help, massage the uterus, IV access with large-bore cannulae, fluids, oxytocin infusion, tranexamic acid within 3 hours, misoprostol or ergometrine, bimanual compression, empty the bladder, examine for tears, and blood transfusion; non-pneumatic anti-shock garment and uterine balloon tamponade can be used while arranging surgery. Pre-eclampsia: hypertension (≥ 140/90) after 20 weeks with proteinuria or organ dysfunction; eclampsia is seizures. Magnesium sulphate is the drug of choice to prevent and treat eclamptic seizures (Pritchard regimen: 4 g IV + 10 g IM loading, then 5 g IM 4-hourly), monitoring respiratory rate (> 16/min), urine output (> 30 mL/h) and patellar reflexes; calcium gluconate is the antidote. Control severe BP (labetalol, hydralazine, nifedipine) and deliver the baby.
k: MgSO4 for eclampsia; monitor RR, urine, reflexes

notes.b: Obstructed labour (common with cephalopelvic disproportion, malpresentation and lack of skilled care) can cause uterine rupture, fistula (vesicovaginal fistula — a major problem in northern Nigeria), sepsis and death; the partograph identifies prolonged labour for timely referral and caesarean section. Puerperal sepsis presents with fever, foul lochia and lower abdominal pain — treat with broad-spectrum antibiotics and source control. Cord prolapse: relieve pressure on the cord (knee–chest or exaggerated Sims' position, fill the bladder, push the presenting part up) and urgent delivery. Neonatal resuscitation (Helping Babies Breathe): dry and stimulate; if not breathing within the 'Golden Minute', clear the airway if needed and give bag-and-mask ventilation (40–60 breaths/min); check heart rate.
k: Cord prolapse: relieve pressure, urgent delivery

topics.title: Postnatal and Newborn Care
topics.summary: Postnatal checks, breastfeeding support, newborn assessment, jaundice and the low-birth-weight baby.

notes.b: Most maternal and neonatal deaths occur around birth and in the first week; WHO recommends postnatal contacts within 24 hours, on day 3, days 7–14 and at 6 weeks. Maternal checks: vital signs, uterine involution (fundus about at the umbilicus after delivery, descending ~1 cm/day and non-palpable abdominally by about 10–14 days), lochia (rubra → serosa → alba), perineum, breasts, bladder and bowel function, mood (baby blues vs postnatal depression and psychosis), family planning and nutrition. Breastfeeding support: correct positioning and attachment, feeding on demand (8–12 times a day), management of engorgement, sore nipples and mastitis.
k: Postnatal contacts: 24 h, day 3, days 7–14, 6 weeks

notes.b: Newborn assessment: Apgar score at 1 and 5 minutes (Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration — 0–10), full examination (fontanelles, palate, spine, hips, genitalia, anus, reflexes such as Moro and rooting), weight. Keep warm (thermal care; hypothermia is a major killer), exclusive breastfeeding, cord care with chlorhexidine, immunisation (BCG, OPV0, HepB0), and danger signs (poor feeding, convulsions, fast breathing ≥ 60/min, chest indrawing, fever or low temperature, lethargy, jaundice on day 1 or extending to palms and soles, umbilical redness). Physiological jaundice appears after 24 hours and resolves in 1–2 weeks; jaundice within 24 hours is pathological (haemolysis — ABO/Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency) and needs urgent assessment; phototherapy and exchange transfusion prevent kernicterus. Low-birth-weight babies (< 2.5 kg) benefit from kangaroo mother care.

topics.title: Care of the Sick Child and IMCI
topics.summary: IMCI assessment, danger signs, pneumonia, diarrhoea and dehydration, malaria and malnutrition in children.

notes.b: Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) assesses children aged 2 months to 5 years systematically: check general danger signs (inability to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions, lethargy or unconsciousness) — any sign requires urgent referral; then assess main symptoms (cough or difficult breathing, diarrhoea, fever, ear problem), nutrition and immunisation status. Classifications are colour-coded: pink (urgent referral), yellow (specific treatment at the facility), green (home care). Fast breathing thresholds: ≥ 50/min at 2–12 months, ≥ 40/min at 12 months–5 years; chest indrawing indicates severe pneumonia. Pneumonia is treated with oral amoxicillin; severe pneumonia is referred.

Diarrhoea: assess dehydration — severe (two of: lethargic/unconscious, sunken eyes, unable to drink or drinks poorly, skin pinch goes back very slowly) needs IV fluids (Plan C: Ringer's lactate 100 mL/kg); some dehydration (restless/irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, skin pinch goes back slowly) needs ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 hours (Plan B); no dehydration — home fluids and ORS (Plan A). Give zinc for 10–14 days and continue feeding. Bloody diarrhoea is treated as dysentery with antibiotics. Fever: test for malaria with an RDT; treat positive uncomplicated cases with an ACT; severe malaria — pre-referral rectal artesunate or IM artesunate and urgent referral. Malnutrition: check for visible severe wasting, oedema of both feet and MUAC (< 11.5 cm = SAM). Nurses also counsel caregivers on feeding and when to return immediately.
k: Severe dehydration: Plan C IV fluids
Some dehydration: Plan B ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 h
